Followed Google Maps like a loyal adventurer, hoping to stumble upon the famous Batu Marhosa—the mysterious stone said to whistle when the wind hits just right. The location pinned? Yes, we arrived. The vibe? A little more “Where’s the batu?” than “marhosa!” To be fair, nature was doing its thing—there were signs of recent changes in the area: uprooted trees, shifts in vegetation, and an overall feeling that the landscape had been rearranged by something (weather? time? overzealous goats?). There was a small stream trickling through, sort of a waterfall if you squint, just like a fellow review had described. Peaceful? Yes. Whistling rocks? Not so much. We poked around a bit, hoping to hear the wind sing through a stone, but it didn’t feel like the kind of place you’d want to start ripping off leaves. More like a spot you pause, take a breath, and then quietly ask Google if maybe the pin’s a little off. So is it the real Batu Marhosa site? Could be. Is it worth the detour? Only if you’re already in Pangururan and feeling curious, cautious, and equipped with a local guided guide. Batu Marhosa might not have whistled for us, but the adventure lives on—just a little further up the trail. Note: If you’re feeling brave, stubborn, and have a heart of steel (and a sturdy bike)—you could venture even further up to Danau Aek Natonang. It’s a crater lake that takes some effort and determination to reach, especially on two wheels. Think gravel, slopes, landslides and a workout for your soul. It’d easily earn you a badge of Samosir explorer pride, and a slice of unknown peace but also magically transported into a near no-mans world that only the locals know

review_text_raw: It was my second visit to this traditional village and this visit was personally dissappointing. The houses, courtyard and sites in the village core were renovated between 2021–2022; thus changing the heritage ambience, modernizing the visiting experience in an unsubtle way. The modernized surroundings made the experience different; renovation of the traditional houses façade and roof, paved courtyard and a modern version of the visitors theatre, submerged the heritage into a less true experience, rather synthetic one. Wandered into the Batak Museum in Tomok expecting the usual museum vibe... but nope, it was completely unmanned when we arrived—zero staff, zero lights. It felt like we had unlocked a bonus level of Night at the Museum: Batak Edition. Cue us creeping around with a mini torch, hunting for light switches like modern-day explorers. (found them, and yes, we felt like heroes.) Once lit, the place came alive. Housed in a beautifully preserved Rumah Bolon (traditional Batak longhouse), the museum showcases a fascinating collection of Batak artifacts—from ulos cloths and weapons to carvings with rich symbolic meaning. Every corner whispers stories of Batak life, rituals, and royal legacy but was short of descriptions and had to be dugged up from the www. Bonus history hit: Tomok is home to the Sidabutar royal tombs, so you’re literally walking through centuries of cultural richness. Note: • Don’t be surprised by the many vendors who would spring at the entrance, surrounding the village are mostly descendants of the Sidabutar family • Bring a flashlight or phone torch just in case you end up like us on a cloudy gloomy day that adds to the spook • Pair it with a visit to the King Sidabutar Tomb and Sigale-gale performance. • Look up the meaning of Batak carvings before you go—it makes everything more meaningful.
